title: Competence element frontmatter
description:
Governs the YAML frontmatter of content/competence/elements/<domain>/<element-id>.md. An element is an ASSESSABLE CLAIM ABOUT A PERSON: what they know, can do, or can judge, and how that would be observed. It is not where the subject is explained — that is a BOK article, and the element points at one through `knowledgeRefs`.

This was one file until decision 38. Merging them produced 2232 assessment-shaped fragments instead of an encyclopedia, duplicated any knowledge serving more than one element, and left the BOK impossible to cite on its own terms. The Markdown body here is now short: notes for assessors and item authors about how the claim is tested. Teaching material belongs in content/bok/.

domain.description: Authoritative domain. If it disagrees with the ID prefix, this field wins — the prefix is historical because IDs never change.

kind.description: Must equal the kind recorded in the taxonomy skeleton. The validator cross-checks. Write the anchors to match: a skill element's anchors describe performance, not understanding.

summary.description: What this element is and why it matters, in the author's own words. Not a definition anyone could look up — the reader has references and an AI assistant open. Say what those cannot: why it matters, where it bites, what practitioners get wrong.

levelCeiling.description: Must equal the ceiling recorded in the taxonomy skeleton. The validator cross-checks.

anchors.description: Observable behavioural anchors, one per attainable level from 1 up to levelCeiling. An anchor describes what a person can be SEEN TO DO for this specific element. 'Understands uncertainty budgets' is not an anchor. 'Constructs a budget for a multi-parameter measurement, identifies correlated inputs, and defends the coverage factor chosen' is.

roleTargets.description:
The MINIMUM proficiency this element requires of each reference role, once the element is within that person's deployment scope. Normative, not descriptive and not aspirational: it states what the role requires, not what holders of it typically reach or would like to reach.

A roleTarget DOES NOT IMPLY APPLICABILITY. It says nothing about whether this element is part of any particular person's work. Applicability comes from a deployment scope (see deployment-scope.schema.json), supplied by an appointment or by the person's own declaration, and AN ELEMENT OUTSIDE SCOPE CANNOT PRODUCE A COMPETENCE GAP. Rate the level the role would need if the element applied; do not try to guess whose job it is.

That separation is what keeps the corpus organization-agnostic. What a 'calibration engineer' covers differs between a dimensional house and a national institute, and the taxonomy has no business deciding.

Use null only where the element could never be part of that role's work IN ANY DEPLOYMENT — a stronger claim than 'not in this person's scope today'. Silence is not the same as null, and the validator will not accept a missing role.

This is also not authorization. What a person is permitted to do is granted by an organization and lives in authorization.schema.json.

citations.description: At least one precise, clause-level source reference is mandatory for every element, whatever the source's licence tier. This is what makes the corpus auditable. NOT necessarily a normative one: accepted practice, emerging technique, research and interpretation are all legitimate, as are adjacent competencies where no clause requires anything of anybody. The standing of the claim is recorded in `currency.authorityStatus`.

quotes.description: Optional, tier-gated. Limits are enforced by the validator against content/sources/registry.yaml, not here.

knowledgeRefs.description:
REQUIRED, at least one. Where a person goes to learn this, and — more importantly — where they go to REMIND themselves. Someone credentialed eight months ago who has forgotten one detail will not retrain; they will look it up, and this is the link that has to work. Section-level rather than article-level for exactly that reason.

This imposes an ordering on authoring, deliberately: the reference material must exist before the claim that someone has mastered it. An element that cannot point at an explanation is an element nobody can prepare for.

demonstration.description:
The routes by which this competence can be evidenced, as a SET. `desk` — the performance is produced with ordinary working tools: a budget, a procedure, a report, an analysis. `equipment` — it requires physical apparatus the learner may not be able to reach: a CMM, gauge blocks, a comparator, a climate chamber.

WHY A SET RATHER THAN A SINGLE VALUE. For most elements there is one route and this array has one entry. For some there are genuinely two, the competence is the same in both, and which one is available is a property of the LABORATORY rather than of the element. Numerical estimation of a sensitivity coefficient is obtained by perturbing a model: where the model is a correction routine or a fitted surface that is desk work, and where it exists only as the instrument itself the perturbation is applied to the instrument and carries its measurement noise, which is bench work. JCGM 100 §5.1.4 contemplates both.

Forcing one value was wrong in both directions, and neither error was silent for the same person. `equipment` alone invents a barrier for every learner who could demonstrate the competence tomorrow against a routine — which lands on exactly the person the Personal edition exists for. `desk` alone hides a real barrier from the learner who will need access, because a module preparing the instrument route could not then declare it.

THIS IS NOT THE SAME AS `kind`, and conflating them was a real error. `skill` means the evidence is observable performance rather than explanation; it does not mean the performance happens at a bench. Constructing an uncertainty budget is a skill and is desk work. Wringing a gauge block stack is a skill and is not.

WHAT IT DECIDES. Whether a training module leaves an element `pending-demonstration`. A module preparing for a single-route element takes the route the element declares and may not restate it. A module preparing for a MULTI-route element MUST say which route it prepares, in `route` on its `preparesFor` entry: the choice may not be made by omission, because silence would leave a learner who needs bench access unwarned while the module still validated.

ORDER IS NOT MEANING. The definition pin sorts this array before hashing, so `[equipment, desk]` and `[desk, equipment]` are the same definition and neither is drift from the other. Defaults to `[desk]`, and omitting the field hashes identically to stating it.

Only meaningful for `skill` elements: knowledge and judgment are evidenced by explanation and defence, which are desk work by definition.

prerequisites.description: Elements a learner should hold before attempting this one. The validator checks the resulting graph is acyclic and every target resolves.

relatedElements.description: Non-blocking cross-references. Use these liberally — the adjacency between, say, an uncertainty element and a technical-writing element is exactly the kind of connection that gets missed.

recertificationMonths.description: How long a credential in this element stays current before recertification. Competence decays, and it decays at different rates — a regulatory element changes with the standard; a fundamental physical principle does not. Omit to inherit the domain default.

currency.description: Knowledge currency. Separates what an element ASSERTS from how far that assertion can be trusted over time. Without this the corpus silently rots: a withdrawn standard reads exactly like a live one, and a reader cannot tell an emerging practice from a settled requirement. REQUIRED. It was previously described as required from Phase 4 onward while being structurally optional, which is exactly how a corpus enters volume authoring full of elements carrying no currency metadata at all. Made structural instead, while one element exists and the cost is nil.

authorityStatus.description: What kind of claim this element makes. normative: a current published requirement a laboratory can be held to. authoritative: settled measurement science, not a requirement — the SI, the GUM framework. accepted-practice: what competent practitioners do, without a standard mandating it. emerging: real and worth knowing but not yet settled. historical: was normative, has been withdrawn or superseded, and is retained because practitioners still encounter it — ANSI/NCSLI Z540.3 is the type case. research: active investigation, no consensus. interpretation: this project's own reading, clearly the author's view rather than anyone's requirement.

volatility.description: How fast this can go out of date, which drives review cadence rather than merely describing it. static: the physics does not change. stable: decade-scale drift. controlled: changes on a published revision cycle, so review is event-driven — a new edition of ISO/IEC 17025 should trigger it, not a calendar. volatile: months, and CM-21 is largely this.

sourceRevision.description: The specific edition or revision the content was written against, when it tracks one. Distinct from the citation's edition: the citation says which clause was consulted, this says which revision the prose currently reflects, and the two diverge exactly when a standard is updated and the content has not caught up.

lastVerified.description: When a competent person last confirmed this is still true. Not when the file was edited — a typo fix is not verification.

reviewDue.description: When it must be looked at again. Derived from volatility unless set explicitly.

supersedes.description: Elements this one replaces. The superseded elements remain in the corpus, deprecated, because content is created and never destroyed — a person credentialed against the old element must still be able to see what they were assessed on.

note.description: Anything a reader needs to know about the standing of this content — a withdrawal, a pending revision, a known disagreement in the field.

reviews.description:
Review provenance for the element itself, distinct from the metrology sources it cites and from the reviews on the BOK articles behind it.

NOT A STATUS FLAG. `bok-article` says it plainly and the reasoning is identical here: there is deliberately no field by which content asserts its own authority, because that is the 'trust me' problem this project exists to solve. An element's standing is DERIVED from who reviewed it, in what capacity, and what they concluded — which is why `authoring.goldReference` is now computed against this array rather than believed.

Elements had no review provenance at all until this existed. `authoring.lastReviewedOn` is a date with nobody attached to it: it records that somebody looked, not who, not at what, and not what they concluded. It is kept for ordinary housekeeping and is not evidence of anything.

reviewType.description:
Technical review says the metrology is right. ASSESSMENT review says the anchors are observable, gradeable, and describe the level they sit on — a different competence, and the one a gold reference is actually exemplary at. Editorial says it reads well.

Kept apart for the reason the article schema gives: conflating them lets a copy-edit masquerade as a technical endorsement. The split matters more on an element than on an article, because an element with impeccable metrology and an unassessable L4 anchor is not a defect a technical reviewer is looking for.

disposition.description: `disputed` is a legitimate outcome and not a failure state: a reviewer who disagrees on substance has told a reader something worth knowing. It does not support a gold reference, which is a different question from whether it is worth recording.

covers.description:
WHICH LEVELS WERE ACTUALLY REVIEWED, pinned by the element definition at that level. Scoped rather than whole-element for the reason an article review is scoped to sections: a reviewer who validated the L1 to L3 anchors in 2026 has not endorsed an L5 anchor rewritten in 2028, and an unscoped review would silently claim they had.

The pin is the same projection a credential's `definitionRef` uses, so a review and a credential go stale on exactly the same edits and neither is disturbed by a typo fix. This is what makes 'gold references are changed reluctantly' executable rather than aspirational: rewrite an anchor and the gold status lapses until somebody reviews it again.

note.description: Required when the disposition is `disputed` or `rejected`. A disagreement with no stated substance is unusable to a reader and unfair to the author.

conflictDisclosed.description: Any commercial or professional interest the reviewer disclosed, per GOVERNANCE.md. Recorded on the element rather than in a side channel, because a reader weighing the review needs it.

authoring.description: Provenance of the content itself, distinct from the metrology sources it cites.

authors.description: Who wrote this element. Optional in general and REQUIRED for a gold reference, because "the reviewer is not the author" cannot be checked against an element that names no author — and an exemplar nobody will put their name to is not one.
